triage.name: Atrial Fibrillation
triage.reason: Very common arrhythmia presenting with palpitations, dyspnea or incidentally; diagnosis by ECG with rich teaching on stroke risk and rate/rhythm management.

rule_errors: workup.not_indicated: unknown test id 'ct_head_without_contrast'; use a listed id or the test's plain name
workup: 'electrocardiogram (12-lead)' appears in ['initial', 'confirmatory']; use one group, or not_indicated plus one entry with only_if

demographics: Risk rises steadily with age; most patients are over 65
More common in people of European ancestry than in other groups
Men are affected somewhat more often than women

risk_factors.text: Valvular heart disease, especially mitral valve disease
COPD and other chronic lung disease
Recent heart, lung, or esophageal surgery
Stimulant drug use such as cocaine or methamphetamine

family_history: Atrial fibrillation in a parent or sibling
exposures: Recent cardiac, lung, or esophageal surgery

chief_complaints.text: My heart is racing and fluttering in my chest
I feel worn out all the time
I get winded just walking to the mailbox
I got lightheaded and nearly passed out
My chest feels tight and uncomfortable
My doctor said my pulse was irregular at my checkup

hpi.onset: Often sudden, over seconds to minutes; sometimes noticed only when a clinician feels an irregular pulse or a monitor is reviewed
hpi.duration: Episodes may last minutes to hours and stop on their own, or the rhythm may stay irregular for days, weeks, or longer
hpi.progression: Variable: some people have brief occasional episodes, others have episodes that become longer and more frequent, and some stay in it continuously
hpi.location: Chest, with the racing or fluttering felt behind the breastbone
hpi.quality: Irregular fluttering, pounding, or a sense that the heart is skipping beats
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate for most; can be severe when the rate is very fast or when heart disease is present
hpi.timing: Comes and goes, or constant; often worse with exertion, after alcohol, or at night
relieving: Nothing reliably stops an episode on its own

associated_symptoms.text: Shortness of breath when lying flat
Swelling in the ankles or legs
Urinating more often, especially at night

pertinent_negatives: Crushing chest pain radiating to the arm or jaw
Sudden one-sided weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking
Recent long car or plane trip with leg swelling

positives.text: Irregular heartbeat noticed by the patient

negatives: Exertional chest pain relieved by rest
Pain radiating to the jaw or arm

atypical.how_it_differs: Many have no palpitations at all and instead present with fatigue, poor exercise tolerance, confusion, falls, or worsening heart failure; the irregular pulse is found on routine exam.
Rare, and usually tied to congenital heart disease, prior cardiac surgery, or an inherited rhythm condition; palpitations and exercise intolerance are the usual clues.
Uncommon; when it occurs it is often linked to hyperthyroidism, structural heart disease, or a prior ablation, and symptoms overlap heavily with normal pregnancy breathlessness.
Symptoms are more often exertional breathlessness and fatigue than palpitations, and episodes are more likely to become persistent.
Silent or minimally symptomatic episodes are more common, so it is often picked up on a routine pulse check or monitor rather than from a complaint.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; may appear well
general.moderate: Mildly anxious or restless, aware of the heartbeat
general.severe: Dyspneic, diaphoretic, sitting upright, visibly uncomfortable
general.critical: Acutely ill, hypotensive, altered mental status, signs of shock or pulmonary edema

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse for at least 30 seconds, assessing rate and rhythm
findings.finding: Irregularly irregular pulse with no repeating pattern

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apical rate while simultaneously palpating the radial pulse
findings.finding: Apical rate exceeds the radial rate (pulse deficit)

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart at the apex and base
findings.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm with variable intensity of S1

findings.maneuver: Count the heart rate by auscultation or pulse
findings.finding: Heart rate greater than 100/min

findings.maneuver: Auscultate at the apex with the bell
findings.finding: Third heart sound suggesting heart failure
Murmur suggesting valvular disease (e.g., mitral regurgitation or stenosis)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein at 45 degrees
findings.finding: Elevated jugular venous pressure
Bibasilar crackles suggesting pulmonary congestion

findings.maneuver: Press the pretibial area and ankles for pitting edema
findings.finding: Bilateral pitting edema

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms
findings.finding: Systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation and level of consciousness
findings.finding: Confusion or reduced alertness from poor perfusion
No goiter or nodule

findings.maneuver: Palpate the calves for tenderness and asymmetry
findings.finding: No calf tenderness or swelling to suggest deep vein thrombosis

findings.maneuver: Screen cranial nerves, strength, and speech
findings.finding: No focal neurologic deficit

labs.caveat: Hyperthyroidism is a reversible driver; check in every new diagnosis, especially with weight loss, heat intolerance, or tremor.
Order with an abnormal TSH to confirm thyrotoxicosis.
Anemia worsens symptoms and can be a sign of occult bleeding, which matters before starting anticoagulation.
Low platelets change the choice and safety of anticoagulation.
Kidney function guides dosing of rate-control drugs and anticoagulants; eGFR is computed from this.
Hypokalemia promotes atrial fibrillation and arrhythmia; correct before or during rate control.
Low magnesium makes potassium hard to correct and lowers the threshold for arrhythmia.
Mild elevations are common with a fast rate alone; a rising or markedly high value points to acute coronary syndrome or demand ischemia.
Supports heart failure as the driver or consequence; higher values track with worse congestion.
Interchangeable with BNP; order one, not both.
Baseline before starting warfarin; an elevated value suggests liver disease or a bleeding tendency.
Baseline before heparin or when a bleeding disorder is suspected.
Diabetes is a major stroke risk factor and affects anticoagulation decisions.
Part of vascular risk assessment, not the diagnosis.
An elevated count suggests infection or another acute trigger for the arrhythmia.
Nonspecific; supports an inflammatory or infectious trigger when the story fits.

findings.finding: Irregularly irregular ventricular response with no repeating pattern
No discrete P waves; instead a fine, chaotic undulating baseline (fibrillatory waves), best seen in V1
Ventricular rate often 100–160/min when untreated; may be normal or slow with rate-control drugs or conduction disease
Narrow QRS unless there is a bundle branch block, aberrancy, or a pre-excited pathway
QT interval varies with the irregular cycle length; measure and correct before starting antiarrhythmic drugs
ST depression or T-wave flattening from a fast rate (demand ischemia); resolves with rate control
Coarse or fine fibrillatory waves with an irregularly irregular response; a regular wide-complex tachycardia should raise concern for ventricular tachycardia or pre-excited atrial fibrillation
Left ventricular hypertrophy or prior Q-wave infarction suggesting underlying structural heart disease

imaging.preferred_when: Every new diagnosis of atrial fibrillation

findings.text: Left ventricular hypertrophy from long-standing hypertension
Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (heart failure)
Normal chamber sizes and function (lone atrial fibrillation)
Intracardiac thrombus, best seen in the left atrial appendage on transesophageal imaging

imaging.preferred_when: Before cardioversion when the duration of atrial fibrillation is over 48 hours or unknown and anticoagulation has not been adequate

findings.text: Spontaneous echo contrast (smoke) in the left atrium
No thrombus, allowing cardioversion to proceed
Pulmonary venous congestion or edema when heart failure is present

imaging.study: CT or MRI of the brain without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: New focal neurologic symptoms or suspected stroke

findings.text: No acute hemorrhage, allowing anticoagulation decisions

imaging.preferred_when: Chest pain with troponin rise suggesting acute coronary syndrome

findings.text: Nonobstructive disease or normal coronaries with demand ischemia from the fast rate

initial.why: Confirms the diagnosis by showing an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves
Anemia, infection, and platelet count before anticoagulation
Potassium, magnesium, and kidney function guide rate control and anticoagulant dosing
Looks for structural heart disease, left atrial size, and ejection fraction
Screens for acute coronary syndrome when chest pain or a very fast rate is present
initial.only_if: chest pain, ischemic ECG changes, or hemodynamic instability

initial.why: Assesses pulmonary congestion and lung disease
initial.only_if: dyspnea, hypoxemia, or suspected heart failure or pneumonia

initial.test: Ambulatory rhythm monitor (Holter or event monitor)
initial.why: Captures paroxysmal episodes not seen on a single ECG
initial.only_if: symptoms are intermittent and the initial ECG is sinus rhythm

confirmatory.why: The diagnostic test; a 12-lead tracing during symptoms is definitive

supporting.why: Supports heart failure as the driver or consequence
Identifies diabetes, a major stroke risk factor
Baseline before heparin or when a bleeding disorder is suspected
Rules out left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion
supporting.only_if: atrial fibrillation has lasted over 48 hours or the duration is unknown and anticoagulation has not been adequate

supporting.test: CT or MRI of the brain without contrast
supporting.only_if: new focal neurologic deficit or altered mental status

not_indicated.why: No role in diagnosing atrial fibrillation; only useful if pulmonary embolism is suspected
Not needed unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Does not help diagnose or manage atrial fibrillation
Not routine; reserve for focal neurologic symptoms or suspected stroke
Not routine; reserve for acute coronary syndrome or refractory ischemia

decision_points: Confirm the rhythm on a 12-lead ECG before treating; a regular wide-complex tachycardia is not atrial fibrillation
Assess hemodynamic stability: hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema, or ischemic chest pain calls for urgent synchronized cardioversion rather than drugs
Estimate stroke risk to decide on anticoagulation, and bleeding risk to choose the agent

If atrial fibrillation has lasted over 48 hours or the duration is unknown, anticoagulate for at least three weeks or exclude left atrial appendage thrombus by transesophageal echocardiogram before elective cardioversion
Look for and treat reversible triggers: hyperthyroidism, infection, alcohol, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and sleep apnea

criteria.name: ECG diagnosis of atrial fibrillation
criteria.summary: An irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm with no consistent P waves and a chaotic fibrillatory baseline; the QRS is usually narrow unless there is conduction disease or pre-excitation.
items: Fibrillatory baseline best seen in V1
Narrow QRS unless bundle branch block or aberrancy

differential.name: Atrial flutter
differential.why_considered: Also causes a fast, irregular-feeling heartbeat in older patients with similar risk factors

history: Palpitations that feel regular but fast
Often paroxysmal and stops abruptly
Similar triggers: alcohol, surgery, lung disease
exam: Pulse may be regular at a fixed rate (e.g., 150/min) or irregular if the block varies
No pulse deficit when the response is fixed
imaging: Echocardiogram shows similar left atrial enlargement
ecg: Sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min, often negative in the inferior leads
Regular atrial activity rather than a chaotic fibrillatory baseline
Ventricular rate often a fixed fraction of the atrial rate

differential.name: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
differential.why_considered: Irregular fast rhythm in older patients, especially with COPD or acute illness

history: Underlying severe lung disease or acute illness
Gradual onset rather than sudden
exam: Irregular pulse but rate usually under 150/min
Signs of COPD: barrel chest, prolonged expiration
labs: Hypoxemia, hypercapnia, theophylline or albuterol use
imaging: Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation or pneumonia
ecg: At least three distinct P-wave shapes with varying P-P intervals
Discrete P waves are present before each QRS
Rate usually 100–130/min

differential.name: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
differential.why_considered: Sudden-onset racing heartbeat in a patient without structural heart disease

history: Abrupt start and stop, often with a single triggering event
Younger patients or those with a known accessory pathway
Neck pounding or a sensation of a switch flipping
exam: Regular, fast pulse that does not vary
No pulse deficit
labs: Usually normal; TSH to exclude thyrotoxicosis
ecg: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150–250/min
P waves hidden in or just after the QRS
No fibrillatory baseline

differential.name: Sinus tachycardia
differential.why_considered: Fast heartbeat with a clear trigger such as fever, pain, dehydration, or anxiety

history: Gradual onset and offset
Obvious trigger: fever, exercise, anemia, pain, anxiety, thyroid disease
exam: Regular pulse that varies with respiration and activity
Signs of the underlying cause (fever, pallor, tremor)
labs: Anemia, hyperthyroidism, or infection on labs
imaging: Echocardiogram normal unless the underlying cause is cardiac
ecg: Regular rhythm with a normal P wave before every QRS
Rate usually under 150/min and falls with treatment of the trigger
P waves upright in lead II

differential.name: Ventricular tachycardia
differential.why_considered: Fast wide-complex rhythm that can be mistaken for atrial fibrillation with aberrancy
differential.trigger: Wide-complex tachycardia with a regular rhythm, especially with known structural heart disease or prior myocardial infarction

history: Prior myocardial infarction or cardiomyopathy
Syncope or near-syncope at onset
Family history of sudden cardiac death
exam: Signs of hemodynamic compromise: hypotension, altered mental status
Cannon A waves in the neck from AV dissociation
labs: Troponin may rise with ischemia; potassium and magnesium abnormalities
imaging: Echocardiogram shows reduced ejection fraction or regional wall-motion abnormality
ecg: Regular wide-complex tachycardia (QRS over 120 ms)
AV dissociation with fusion or capture beats
Concordant precordial pattern or extreme axis

differential.name: Pre-excited atrial fibrillation (Wolff-Parkinson-White)
differential.why_considered: Irregular fast rhythm that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation if AV-nodal blockers are given
differential.trigger: Irregular wide-complex tachycardia with rates over 200/min in a younger patient or one with a known accessory pathway

history: Prior episodes of rapid palpitations
Younger age without structural heart disease
Family history of sudden death
exam: Very fast irregular pulse, often over 200/min
Signs of poor perfusion
labs: Usually normal; TSH to exclude thyrotoxicosis
imaging: Echocardiogram may be normal or show Ebstein anomaly
ecg: Irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia with varying QRS width
Short PR interval and delta wave in sinus rhythm
Rates can exceed 200/min

differential.name: Atrial fibrillation with aberrancy or bundle branch block
differential.why_considered: Irregular wide-complex rhythm that can be mistaken for ventricular tachycardia

history: Known prior bundle branch block on old ECGs
No syncope at onset
exam: Irregularly irregular pulse
Hemodynamics usually stable
ecg: Irregularly irregular rhythm with wide QRS of consistent morphology
Fibrillatory baseline in V1
QRS morphology matches a prior bundle branch block pattern

differential.name: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response from thyrotoxicosis
differential.why_considered: Fast irregular rhythm driven by a reversible endocrine cause

history: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, diarrhea, anxiety
Recent iodine load or amiodarone use
exam: Goiter, lid lag, fine tremor, warm moist skin
Wide pulse pressure
labs: Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 or T3
imaging: Thyroid ultrasound or uptake scan if a nodule is found
ecg: Atrial fibrillation that may be resistant to rate control until thyroid is treated

differential.name: Atrial fibrillation triggered by alcohol or stimulant use
differential.why_considered: Binge drinking or stimulant use commonly precipitates paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in otherwise healthy people

history: Binge drinking or cocaine/methamphetamine use before episodes
Episodes cluster on weekends or after parties
Younger than typical atrial fibrillation patients
exam: Signs of intoxication or withdrawal
Tachycardia and hypertension during use
labs: Elevated ethanol level, positive urine drug screen, elevated AST/ALT or GGT
ecg: Atrial fibrillation that often converts with abstinence and rate control

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Sudden dyspnea, chest discomfort, and tachycardia can mimic atrial fibrillation, and PE can trigger it
differential.trigger: Acute dyspnea with hypoxemia, pleuritic chest pain, or recent immobilization, surgery, or cancer

history: Recent long travel, surgery, or immobility
Pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis
Unilateral leg swelling or pain
exam: Tachypnea, hypoxemia, clear lungs
Unilateral calf tenderness or swelling
Signs of right heart strain: elevated JVP, loud P2
labs: Troponin and BNP elevation from right heart strain
imaging: CT pulmonary angiography shows filling defect in pulmonary arteries
Lower-extremity ultrasound may show deep vein thrombosis
ecg: Sinus tachycardia most common; may show S1Q3T3, right axis deviation, or right bundle branch block
Atrial fibrillation can be present as a consequence

differential.name: Acute coronary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chest discomfort with a fast irregular rhythm and troponin elevation can be due to ischemia or demand
differential.trigger: Chest pressure, diaphoresis, or ischemic ECG changes in a patient with vascular risk factors

history: Crushing substernal chest pressure radiating to arm or jaw
Diaphoresis, nausea, exertional onset
Prior coronary disease or stents
exam: Diaphoresis, anxiety, S3 or new murmur
Signs of heart failure
imaging: Echocardiogram may show new regional wall-motion abnormality
ecg: ST depression or elevation, T-wave inversions in a coronary distribution
Ischemic changes persist after rate control, unlike demand ischemia

differential.name: Sepsis or acute infection
differential.why_considered: Infection is a common trigger for new atrial fibrillation in hospitalized or older patients

history: Fever, cough, dysuria, or abdominal pain
Recent hospitalization or procedure
Immunosuppression
exam: Fever or hypothermia, hypotension, altered mental status
Focal source: crackles, abdominal tenderness, costovertebral angle tenderness
labs: Leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, positive cultures
imaging: CT or ultrasound identifies the source
ecg: Atrial fibrillation often resolves with treatment of the infection

severity.mild: Paroxysmal episodes with a controlled rate, minimal symptoms, and no heart failure; often found incidentally on a routine pulse check
severity.moderate: Persistent or frequently symptomatic atrial fibrillation with a rate over 100/min, fatigue, exertional dyspnea, or mild congestion but stable hemodynamics
severity.severe: Rapid ventricular response with hypotension, pulmonary congestion, or ischemic chest pain that needs urgent rate control or cardioversion
severity.critical: Hemodynamic collapse, shock, pulmonary edema, or acute stroke from embolization; needs immediate synchronized cardioversion or stroke pathway activation

red_flags.finding: Systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg or signs of shock
red_flags.meaning: Unstable atrial fibrillation; proceed to urgent synchronized cardioversion rather than drugs
Loss of atrial kick and rapid rate causing heart failure; needs urgent rate control or cardioversion

red_flags.finding: Ischemic chest pain with ST changes
red_flags.meaning: Acute coronary syndrome or demand ischemia; treat ischemia and rate together

red_flags.finding: New focal neurologic deficit, facial droop, or trouble speaking
red_flags.meaning: Cardioembolic stroke; activate the stroke pathway and image the brain
Poor perfusion from a very fast rate, conduction disease, or another arrhythmia

red_flags.finding: Pre-excited atrial fibrillation (irregular wide-complex tachycardia over 200/min)
red_flags.meaning: Risk of ventricular fibrillation; avoid AV-nodal blockers and use electrical cardioversion

complications.name: Cardioembolic stroke
clues: Sudden focal weakness, numbness, or speech difficulty
Left atrial enlargement or thrombus on echo
High stroke risk score and no anticoagulation

complications.name: Heart failure from tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy
clues: Weeks to months of uncontrolled rate
Progressive dyspnea, edema, and reduced ejection fraction
Improves with rate or rhythm control

complications.name: Systemic embolism (limb or mesenteric)
clues: Sudden cold, painful limb with absent pulses
Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam

complications.name: Acute decompensated heart failure
clues: Rapid rate with crackles, elevated JVP, and edema

complications.name: Bleeding from anticoagulation
clues: Supratherapeutic INR or recent NSAID use

complications.name: Sudden cardiac arrest
clues: Pre-excited atrial fibrillation with very fast rates
Severe structural heart disease or electrolyte disturbance

special_populations.differences: Often presents without palpitations, with fatigue, falls, confusion, or worsening heart failure; higher stroke risk and higher bleeding risk, so anticoagulation decisions need careful weighing.

Uncommon; when present, look for hyperthyroidism, structural heart disease, or prior ablation. Rate-control and anticoagulation choices must account for fetal safety, and delivery planning involves a multidisciplinary team.

Rare and usually linked to congenital heart disease, prior cardiac surgery, or an inherited rhythm condition; palpitations and exercise intolerance are the usual clues, and management is by pediatric cardiology.
Kidney function guides dosing of rate-control drugs and anticoagulants; direct oral anticoagulants may be dose-adjusted or avoided, and warfarin may be preferred in advanced disease.
Symptoms are more often exertional breathlessness and fatigue than palpitations; episodes are more likely to become persistent, and weight loss reduces burden.
Silent or minimally symptomatic episodes are more common, so it is often picked up on a routine pulse check or monitor; diabetes adds to stroke risk and affects anticoagulation decisions.

key_questions.question: What does the racing or fluttering feel like, and did it start suddenly or gradually?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset of an irregular fluttering or pounding; gradual onset with a clear trigger suggests sinus tachycardia

key_questions.question: When did it start, and is it still going on now?
key_questions.looking_for: Duration under or over 48 hours, which changes the cardioversion plan; ongoing versus resolved

key_questions.question: How often do these episodes happen, and how long do they last?
key_questions.looking_for: Paroxysmal brief episodes versus persistent or permanent rhythm

key_questions.question: What were you doing when it started?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset at rest or with exertion; after alcohol, caffeine, poor sleep, or acute illness

key_questions.question: Do you feel short of breath, lightheaded, or like you might pass out?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspnea, near-syncope, or syncope suggesting poor perfusion or instability

key_questions.question: Any chest pain or pressure?
key_questions.looking_for: Ischemic chest discomfort that would push toward urgent cardioversion and an ACS workup

key_questions.question: How is your energy level and exercise tolerance compared with before?
key_questions.looking_for: Fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance, the most common symptoms

key_questions.question: Do you get short of breath lying flat, or wake up gasping at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea suggesting heart failure

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swelling in your ankles or legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Volume overload from heart failure or valve disease

key_questions.question: Have you had any sudden weakness on one side, numbness, trouble speaking, or vision loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Cardioembolic stroke or TIA; activates the stroke pathway

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, heart failure, valve disease, diabetes, kidney disease, or sleep apnea?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that drive atrial fibrillation and raise stroke risk

key_questions.question: Have you ever had this rhythm before, or a cardioversion or ablation?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior episodes and prior rhythm-control procedures

key_questions.question: Have you had recent surgery on your heart, lungs, or esophagus?
key_questions.looking_for: Postoperative atrial fibrillation in the early days to weeks after surgery

key_questions.question: What medicines do you take, including over-the-counter ones?
key_questions.looking_for: Levothyroxine, albuterol, pseudoephedrine, or other stimulants that can trigger the rhythm

key_questions.question: Do you take any blood thinners?
key_questions.looking_for: Current anticoagulation, which changes the urgency and safety of cardioversion

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink in a typical week, and do you ever binge?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy or binge drinking as a trigger and a modifiable risk factor

key_questions.question: Do you use cocaine, methamphetamine, or other stimulants?
key_questions.looking_for: Stimulant use as a precipitant, especially in younger patients

key_questions.question: Do you smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking as a vascular risk factor

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have atrial fibrillation or heart disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of atrial fibrillation or inherited heart disease

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, cough, burning with urination, or another recent illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Infection as an acute trigger for new atrial fibrillation

key_questions.question: Have you noticed weight loss, heat intolerance, jitteriness, or tremor?
key_questions.looking_for: Hyperthyroidism as a reversible driver

key_questions.question: Have you had any black or bloody stools, unusual bruising, or bleeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Occult bleeding that matters before starting anticoagulation

reasoning_points: An irregularly irregular pulse with no repeating pattern on palpation and auscultation
A 12-lead ECG showing irregularly irregular R-R intervals with no discrete P waves and a fibrillatory baseline best seen in V1
Symptoms of palpitations, fatigue, and exertional dyspnea in a patient with typical risk factors such as older age and hypertension
Reversible triggers considered and addressed: hyperthyroidism, infection, alcohol or stimulant use, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and sleep apnea
Hemodynamic stability assessed, since hypotension, pulmonary edema, or ischemic chest pain calls for urgent synchronized cardioversion
Stroke risk estimated to decide on anticoagulation, and bleeding risk weighed to choose the agent
Duration of the episode established, because over 48 hours or unknown duration requires anticoagulation or a transesophageal echocardiogram before elective cardioversion
Structural heart disease evaluated with a transthoracic echocardiogram

easy: Older adult with hypertension and palpitations
ECG shows no P waves with a chaotic baseline
medium: Older adult with no palpitations, presenting with fatigue, falls, or confusion
Paroxysmal episodes with a normal ECG in the office, requiring an ambulatory monitor
Atrial fibrillation found during an acute infection or after surgery
Rate-controlled atrial fibrillation with a normal ventricular rate on presentation
hard: Irregular wide-complex tachycardia over 200/min suggesting pre-excited atrial fibrillation, where AV-nodal blockers are dangerous
Atrial fibrillation with aberrancy mistaken for ventricular tachycardia
Thyrotoxicosis driving the rhythm and resisting rate control until the thyroid is treated
Younger patient whose episodes are triggered by binge alcohol or stimulant use with an otherwise normal workup
Unstable atrial fibrillation with hypotension or pulmonary edema requiring immediate cardioversion
